strengths: Novel theoretical perspective: The paper establishes a clear mathematical connection between the perturbed objective in Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) and implicit entropy regularization, providing a principled explanation for why SAM counteracts overconfidence.

Empirical verification of theoretical assumptions: The authors explicitly verify the Hessian eigenvalue condition and the bounds on lambda across training trajectories for realistic architectures (ResNet-56 on CIFAR, ViT on ImageNet-1K), lending credibility to the theoretical analysis.

Extensive and rigorous evaluation: The empirical study evaluates multiple architectures (ResNets, WideResNets, PyramidNets, ViTs) across in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-1K, ImageNet-C, SVHN), benchmarking against a broad suite of modern calibration methods (Focal Loss variants, mixup, BalCAL, bSAM, BNNs).

Effective proposed method (CSAM): The derived variant, CSAM, consistently achieves superior calibration metrics (ECE, AdaECE, ClasswiseECE, TCE) without compromising generalization accuracy, addressing the trade-off commonly faced by loss-regularization methods.
weaknesses: Computational overhead: As with vanilla SAM, CSAM relies on two forward-backward passes per optimization step. Comparing calibration efficiency against single-pass calibration approaches (e.g., standard focal loss, label smoothing, or post-hoc calibration) in terms of wall-clock training time would provide a more complete practical picture.

Nature of the theoretical guarantee: Theorem 1 and Theorem 3 provide lower bounds on the perturbed loss rather than exact equivalence, meaning that minimizing the perturbed loss does not formally guarantee minimization of the negative entropy term in every regime.

Heuristic design of the outer loss: The specific weighting factor (1 + \tilde{p}_y)^{-\gamma} in Eq. (4) is largely engineered to yield the bound in Theorem 3; additional ablations comparing this specific modulation against standard focal modulation or direct entropy penalties on perturbed predictions would strengthen the justification.

strengths: Compelling and insightful topic: While SAM is widely known for boosting generalization, its strong calibration benefits have remained under-explored. The paper offers a timely and principled investigation into this phenomenon.

Theoretical connection to entropy regularization: The authors establish that SAM's perturbed loss provides a lower-bound formulation linking SAM to maximum-entropy regularization (analogous to the focal loss connection), providing formal intuition for why SAM counteracts overconfidence.

Well-motivated algorithm: Building on the insight that SAM primarily penalizes overconfidence late in training, the proposed Calibrated SAM (CSAM) adapts the outer loss to further suppress overconfidence, yielding consistent empirical gains.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The paper conducts comprehensive evaluations across multiple architectures (ResNet-20/50/56, WRN-28-10, PyramidNet-110, ViT-S/16, ViT-S/32) and datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1K), including out-of-distribution evaluation under corruptions (CIFAR-10-C, ImageNet-C, SVHN).

Thorough benchmarking: The empirical validation benchmarks against a large variety of calibration techniques (Focal Loss, AdaFocal, DualFocal, Mixup, MIT-L, MMCE, ACLS, BalCAL, MBLS) as well as ensemble and Bayesian approaches (MIMO, BatchEnsemble, Rank1-BNN, bSAM).
weaknesses: Lower-bound minimization logic: Theorems 1-3 provide lower bounds of the form $\ell_{\tilde{\theta}} \ge \ell_\theta - \lambda H(p_y) + H(\tilde{p}_y)$. In optimization, minimizing an upper quantity (the perturbed loss) does not strictly guarantee the maximization of an implicit entropy regularizer in its lower bound. The paper would benefit from toning down claims that SAM is mathematically proven to maximize predictive entropy, framing it instead as a variational/regularization proxy similar to the argument in focal loss literature.

Computational overhead consideration: Like vanilla SAM, CSAM incurs two forward-backward passes per iteration, effectively doubling the training compute compared to single-pass calibration approaches (e.g., Focal Loss, Label Smoothing). A clear discussion of the training wall-clock time and compute-accuracy-calibration trade-offs in the main text is missing.

Heuristic nature of the CSAM outer loss: The specific functional form $(1 + \tilde{p}_y)^{-\gamma} \log \tilde{p}_y$ for $\tilde{p}_y > 0.5$ is somewhat ad hoc. While Theorem 3 shows an entropy-weighting property, an ablation or discussion comparing this modulation to other confidence-discounting forms (such as standard focal weight $(1 - \tilde{p}_y)^\gamma$) would strengthen the algorithmic justification.

strengths: Important and well-motivated research question: while SAM is widely recognized for boosting generalization, its impact on model calibration and predictive uncertainty has not been systematically investigated from a theoretical angle.

Insightful theoretical framing: connecting SAM's worst-case parameter perturbation to an implicit entropy regularization mechanism (analogous to the interpretation of focal loss) offers an intuitive conceptual explanation for why SAM mitigates overconfidence.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper validates claims across multiple architectures (ResNet, WideResNet, PyramidNet, Vision Transformers) on both in-distribution datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1K) and out-of-distribution / corrupted benchmarks (CIFAR-C, SVHN, ImageNet-C).

Thorough benchmarking against calibration baselines: SAM and the proposed CSAM are compared against a broad spectrum of calibration-oriented losses (Focal Loss, AdaFocal, DualFocal, Label Smoothing, ACLS, MMCE, BalCAL) and Bayesian / ensemble baselines (MIMO, Rank1-BNN, bSAM), demonstrating competitive calibration without the typical drop in classification accuracy.
weaknesses: Theoretical gap regarding optimization dynamics: Theorem 1 provides a lower bound on the perturbed loss containing the entropy terms ($\ell_{\tilde{\theta}}(z) \ge \ell_\theta(z) - \lambda H(p_y) + H(\tilde{p}_y)$). However, minimizing an objective function does not theoretically guarantee the minimization or maximization of components in its lower bound. While this provides a heuristic analogy similar to prior work on focal loss, presenting it as a formal proof of implicit entropy maximization is an overstatement.

Strong Hessian boundedness assumptions: Lemmas 1 and 2 rely on the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian along the interpolation segment between $\theta$ and $\tilde{\theta}$ being lower-bounded by $-\|\nabla \ell\|/\rho$. While empirical checks on checkpoints are provided, this condition is non-trivial and may fail in highly non-convex, overparameterized regimes or when larger perturbation radii $\rho$ are chosen.

Compute and wall-clock time comparisons are omitted: SAM and CSAM require two backward passes per iteration, effectively doubling the computational cost per training step compared to standard SGD and single-pass calibration losses (e.g., Focal Loss, Label Smoothing, ACLS). The baselines should be evaluated under compute-matched settings (e.g., training for 2x epochs).

Ad-hoc formulation of CSAM: The proposed modification in Equation (4) introduces a piecewise weighting scheme conditioned on $\tilde{p}_y > 0.5$ and an additional hyperparameter $\gamma$. The transition introduces a derivative discontinuity at $\tilde{p}_y = 0.5$, and the functional form $(1+\tilde{p}_y)^{-\gamma}$ appears heuristically designed rather than derived from a first-principles optimization objective.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically significant and relevant question: explaining why Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) produces well-calibrated predictions and leveraging this insight to design better calibration-aware optimization methods.

The empirical evaluation is extensive, spanning multiple architectures (ResNet, WideResNet, PyramidNet, ViT), datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1K), and settings including in-distribution, out-of-distribution (SVHN), and corrupted data (CIFAR-C, ImageNet-C).

The paper provides insightful practical investigations, such as exploring the effect of the perturbation radius $\rho$ on calibration and studying the transition dynamics (SGD $\to$ SAM vs. SAM $\to$ SGD), showing that SAM is most critical in the later stages of training.
The proposed CSAM is simple to implement and demonstrates consistent reductions in ECE across several benchmark architectures on CIFAR and Tiny-ImageNet compared to existing calibration techniques.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant topic: understanding and enhancing the calibration performance of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM).

The empirical evaluation is broad, testing multiple calibration metrics (ECE, Adaptive ECE, Classwise ECE, Temperature-calibrated ECE, and AUROC) across diverse architectures (ResNets, WideResNets, PyramidNets, ViTs) and under distribution shift (CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, SVHN, ImageNet-C).

The paper includes comparisons against a solid set of calibration baselines, including focal loss variants (DualFocal, AdaFocal), Mixup/MIT-L, MMCE, and probabilistic methods (BatchEnsemble, Rank-1 BNN, MIMO, bSAM).

The theoretical motivation provided for CSAM does not logically follow from the inequality.

CSAM is restricted to CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny-ImageNet, leaving open whether the proposed modification scales effectively to larger datasets.

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: Connecting sharpness-aware optimization with predictive uncertainty and model calibration is an important problem for reliable machine learning.

Extensive empirical exploration of vanilla SAM: The paper provides a thorough empirical benchmark comparing SAM and SGD across architectures (ResNets, ViTs), post-hoc calibrators, and under covariate shift / corruptions (CIFAR-C, ImageNet-C).
Empirical effectiveness of CSAM on small benchmarks: The proposed CSAM heuristic shows lower ECE compared to standard baselines on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny-ImageNet without degrading accuracy.

Surrogate / lower bound fallacy in Theorem 1 and Theorem 2: The paper claims SAM implicitly regularizes the predictive entropy because Theorem 1 establishes a lower bound $\ell_{\tilde{\theta}}(z) \ge \ell_\theta(z) - \lambda H(p_y) + H(\tilde{p}_y)$. Incremental algorithmic novelty: The fact that flat minima optimizers and SAM improve calibration is already known in the literature (e.g., Möllenhoff & Khan, 2023). The proposed CSAM modification amounts to multiplying the loss of confident examples ($\tilde{p}_y > 0.5$) by $(1 + \tilde{p}_y)^{-\gamma}$, which is a heuristic focal-loss-like sample downweighting applied at the perturbed point.

Incomplete evaluation of CSAM: While the abstract emphasizes ImageNet-1K, CSAM is not evaluated on ImageNet-1K at all (Table 2 only compares SGD/AdamW with standard SAM). Furthermore, on CIFAR-100 (Table 4), the calibration gain of CSAM over vanilla SAM is marginal (ECE $1.93\% \pm 0.15\%$ vs. $2.11\% \pm 0.17\%$).
